World's Only Targa Top Barracuda Was Made in 1964 as a Styling Exercise, It's Ridiculously Cheap Now
96 photos
Photo: Bring A Trailer/PatsRareRides
Plymouth is long gone, but its legacy will live for as long as there will be cars and car nuts. The low-cost ChryCo division has the often-overlooked merit of debuting the pony car - ironically called after the Ford Mustang that succeeded the Barracuda by two weeks in April 1964. It also has the merit of creating the first American car with a Targa Top (not to be confused with T-tops): the 1964 Plymouth Barracuda Landau. The only one ever made. This one.
Typically, old cars depreciate in value after a while, right around the time they become “old cars” for the first time. No, I didn’t just shoot myself in the foot with a one-bore grammar-filled slug. Old cars have different degrees of “old.” They’re “just old cars” at first (that no one wants), then they’re “old cars” that are cool, but not really worth much, and then they’re “old cars” worth either their scrap value, or their weight in gold.
Some of those old cars make spectacular comebacks. Anyone care to explain the Hemicuda convertible and their seven-figure sale prices? I'll wait. But not all super-rare and roofless Barracudas are worth millions. This one seen in the gallery - and in the video attached below - isn't even on the “good deal” side of four figures (from a seller’s standpoint), despite being the only one ever made.
That shocking affordability has followed this one-off “corporate design study” across multiple auction blocks. According to the Hagerty Price Guide, the prototype appeared at the RM Sotheby's Auburn Fall auction in September 2010, where it went unsold at a $24,000 high bid. After 16 years, on September 26, 2026, it crossed the Mecum Nashville block for just $21,000 (buyer paid $23,100).
Photo: Bring A Trailer/PatsRareRides As of now, it has a high bid of $22,500 on Bring A Trailer (with four days left), where it will go without reserve. The selling dealer explained the no-reserve listing decision: "It was selling at the end of the auction on Saturday. [September 26]. Late entry to the auction with no marketing. The seats were empty. Empty as in 95% of the crowd gone. When it sold even I couldn’t believe it. IMO BaT is the best platform to sell a unique prototype like this. That is why I chose to sell it without reserve."
Built on the final Thursday of 1964 production, this Valiant-based fastback was immediately requisitioned by Chrysler stylists, who removed the main steel roof panel to test an open-air Landau concept while keeping the arched rear roof hoop – and its signature back window (the largest single piece of glass fitted to a production passenger car).
Finished from the factory in code A Gold and repainted under prior ownership, the exterior features a split grille, front vent windows, V8 fender badges, a deck-lid Valiant emblem, reverse lights, and wraparound chrome bumpers. It rides on 13-inch steel wheels with styled covers and National Horizon polyester whitewalls, showing chipped paint and pitted brightwork.
Photo: Bring A Trailer/PatsRareRides Under the hood sits a 273-cubic-inch LA V8 fed by a Carter two-barrel carburetor, factory rated at 180 horsepower at 4,200 rpm and 260 lb-ft of torque at 1,600 rpm. Power reaches the rear wheels through a push-button TorqueFlite 3-speed automatic transmission, while power-assisted 4-wheel drum brakes boast a new master cylinder.
Inside, gold vinyl covers the worn front bucket seats and fold-down rear bench alongside a Valiant Transaudio AM radio.
A three-spoke steering wheel fronts a 110-mph speedometer and an odometer showing 52,446 miles, (15 miles added by the seller in their sole month of ownership). The white fabric roof panel is damaged and fits poorly, prompting Bring a Trailer commenters to joke about spending beer tokens fabricating a weather-tight top that stays attached at speed. Curiously, the top seemed to be holding on quite well back when the car was photographed for the Mecum listing. Maybe the seller has more details.
Photo: Mecum Sharp-eyed readers also spotted smoothed rear quarter-to-valance seams, crumbling seat foam, and an open gap behind the door glass.
Mopar experts in the comments also diagnosed the car's electrical and suspension quirks. The two non-working gauges for gas and coolant temperature likely stem from a failed voltage limiter, a common issue that is the culprit when both gauges fail. Meanwhile, the hunched stance with the lowered front is probably due to the torsion bar setting.
It should be a straightforward and fairly simple fix: crank the torsion bars to factory specs and this Barracuda will look great again. Speaking of looks, let’s set things straight about the body style. This Barracuda Landau is a Targa top, not a T-top and not a convertible. A Targa top uses a full-width removable panel ahead of a fixed roll bar bridging the B-pillars while retaining the rear glass.
Photo: Bring A Trailer/PatsRareRides Before Porsche trademarked the Targa name after Sicily's Targa Florio race for its 1966-model 911 amid fears of a federal convertible ban, Giovanni Michelotti pioneered the layout on the 1957 Fiat 1200 Wonderful.
Michelotti reprised that idea on the 1961 Triumph TR4, followed by the 1964 Saab Catherina, this 1964 Barracuda, the 1965 Toyota Sports 800, the 1971 Fiat X1/9, Griffith's 1978 Celica Sunchaser and 1981 AMC Eagle Sundancer, and every Corvette coupe since 1984. Conversely, T-tops use split panels divided by a fixed center bar running lengthwise from the windshield to the rear.
This T-tops arrangement was invented by Gordon Buehrig on the airplane-inspired 1948 TASCO prototype (The American Sportscar Company), and patented in 1951.
Photo: Mecum After lying dormant for 20 years, T-tops ignited a craze when General Motors introduced them on the 1968 Corvette, prompting a patent lawsuit from Buehrig. Touted as taking 10 seconds to lift off, T-top Corvettes outsold roadsters and killed the convertible after 1975 until 1986. Throughout the 1970s, T-tops spread across Detroit on the 1975 Hurst/Olds, 1976 Trans Am, 1978 Camaro, Buick Regal, Chrysler Cordoba, Dodge Magnum, Ford Thunderbird, and Mustang.
Despite testing this open-roof Landau in 1964, Plymouth never built a first-generation drop-top, waiting until the 1967 redesign to launch the first factory Barracuda convertible, totaling 4,228 units. All first-gen pony Mopars remained fixed-roof fastbacks.
Following its April 1, 1964 debut, Plymouth produced 23,443 units before the regular 1965 production year began, totaling 64,596 cars during the actual 1965 model year, offering versatile Slant-Six and small-block V8 engine choices.
Photo: Bring A Trailer/PatsRareRides After dropping 1964's 101-horsepower 170-cubic-inch Slant-6, the 1965 lineup featured a 145-horsepower 225-cubic-inch Slant-Six, the 180-horsepower 273-cubic-inch two-barrel V8, and a 235-horsepower 273-cubic-inch four-barrel Commando V8.
Transmission choices included a column-shifted 3-speed manual, a floor-shifted 4-speed manual, or the 3-speed TorqueFlite automatic. With a V8-powered Barracuda carrying a base price of $2,493 in 1964 and $2,571 in 1965, how much do you think a factory Targa-top Barracuda would have cost back then?
